Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette:
Karim was 38, a single Middle Eastern hairdresser who had built his life around being calm, precise, and in control of his hands. Before the illness, his work was the kind that depended on steady attention: mixing color, checking a line, leaning close to a client’s head, catching details in the mirror before anyone else did. He had taken pride in the routine of the salon, the smell of shampoo and dye, the small talk, the sense that he could make people feel better about themselves. When he became seriously ill, that ordinary world narrowed abruptly around hospital corridors, bright lights, and the fear that his own body was failing him.

The illness itself had become frightening in a way Karim still found hard to describe without losing his composure. He had been examined repeatedly, prodded, scanned, and monitored, and at one point he believed his condition could have ended his life. What stayed with him most was not a single dramatic image but the experience of his body: the tense waiting before procedures, the sharp awareness of sensations inside him, and the sense that something dangerous could be happening without warning. Since then, being in a medical examination or procedure has become a potent trigger. He can feel himself brace the moment a clinician tells him to lie back, and he becomes intensely aware of every touch, every instrument, every pause in a doctor’s voice. Even now, he watches his body closely in those settings, certain that it may betray him again.

After he recovered enough to return to work, Karim expected relief to follow. Instead, certain reminders began landing with unexpected force. A customer once showed him photos from a family gathering, and one image of a cousin in a hospital bed left him suddenly flooded with the same dread he had felt during the illness. He described staring at the phone and feeling as if the picture had pulled him back into that period, not because the image itself was dramatic, but because it carried him straight into the knowledge of what had happened to him. At other times, he would wake from a nightmare with no clear picture left in mind, only the residue of terror and a pounding body. Those mornings were especially unsettling because he often knew only that he had been frightened, not what he had dreamed, and the feeling could linger for hours.

At times the memory came without any clear image at all. Karim spoke of suddenly being overwhelmed by the full emotional force of the event while standing at the sink at work or folding towels at home, as if the fear, helplessness, and horror had arrived in his chest before any story could form around them. He also noticed that when he thought about the illness, he could sometimes smell the same hospital odor he associated with that period, a sharp sterile scent that seemed to appear in his mind with no warning. At those moments, his attention fixed on his body. He felt pain returning in the same parts of him that had hurt during the illness, and that sensation made the memory feel immediate and physically real, not like something over and finished.

Over the months, Karim became more convinced that his body was not trustworthy. He had come to believe that it still behaved as if danger were present even when he was sitting safely in the salon or in his apartment. His muscles stayed tense, his body always ready to react, and he was aware of strong physical surges whenever something reminded him of the illness. The reactions frightened him in their own right. He said that part of what upset him most was the thought that his fear itself meant something was wrong with him mentally, that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy. He did not say this lightly; it reflected the distress he felt when the sensations arrived without warning and seemed bigger than the situation in front of him.

These experiences began to affect daily life in practical ways. In the salon, Karim found himself uneasy when clients mentioned medical visits or showed him photos from hospitals or family illness. He became more guarded in conversation and more likely to step away to the back room if he felt his chest tighten or his body start to react. He still worked, but he did so with increasing effort, trying to keep his composure while monitoring himself for signs that another wave might hit. Friends noticed that he seemed less available, and he found himself declining gatherings where talk could drift toward illness or where he might be asked about his own health.

He finally sought help after waking from another nightmare and then having a wave of bodily fear later the same day during a routine medical examination. The combination left him shaken and ashamed, as if he could no longer rely on his own reactions to tell him what was real. What he most hoped for was to be able to trust his body again and to sit through ordinary medical care without feeling as though danger had returned. What frightened him most was the possibility that these intense reactions would keep happening indefinitely, proving to him that his body was still not on his side.
